layout.text: An independent design studio making identities, books and websites for culture and commerce.

children.text: Norma is an independent design studio in Rotterdam. We make identities, books, packaging, websites and spaces for cultural institutions, hospitality and independent brands.

$media.alt: A plywood table on orange trestle legs and a metal stool in a white studio, with sunlight falling across the wall

content.alt: A plywood table on orange trestle legs and a metal stool in a white studio, with sunlight falling across the wall
content.caption: The long table in the studio, where most projects start on paper

children.text: Names, wordmarks and the systems that carry them.
Magazines, catalogues and books, from format to final proof.
Labels, bags and boxes that are cheap to run and easy to change.
Websites and online shops, built to be maintained by the people who use them.
Photography and image-making for campaigns and products.

We keep the studio small on purpose. One of the founders leads every project from the first conversation to the last proof, and most are designed by two or three people. We take on fewer projects so that we can see each one through to production.

We start with what already exists: the building, the archive, the way a business actually runs. Most of what we design is used day to day by the people who commissioned it, so we hand over templates and short guides instead of thick manuals, and check in a few months later to see what needs adjusting.

Norma is five people in a former printworks in Delfshaven. Marit Hoekstra and Felix Aalbers founded the studio in 2019, she from book publishing and he from an architecture practice. They work with the designers Jun Park and Sara Belhaj and the studio manager Pim de Wit.

The name is Latin for a carpenter's square, the L-shaped tool used to check that a frame is true. It describes the job well. Most of our work is making sure things line up, from a grid to a sign on a wall, so that whatever sits inside the frame can be seen clearly.

data.title: North Bakehouse
data.summary: A one-colour identity for a sourdough bakery in Rotterdam-Noord, stamped by hand onto kraft bags every morning.

$media.alt: Two floured sourdough loaves with diagonal scores, side by side on a wooden board

children.text: North Bakehouse opened in 2022 in a former butcher's shop in Rotterdam-Noord. Lotte Brouwer bakes four kinds of loaf every day with grain milled at a windmill in Schiedam. She asked us for an identity that would cost almost nothing to run and still hold its own on a busy street.

We drew a compact wordmark and had it cut into a rubber stamp 60 millimetres wide. Every bag, box and sheet of wrapping paper is unbleached kraft, stamped in one deep blue by whoever opens the shop. There is no printed packaging to reorder and nothing to throw away when the range changes, and the small differences from one impression to the next became part of the identity rather than a fault to correct.
A label that tells the time

Each loaf leaves with a narrow paper band giving its name and the time it came out of the oven. The bands come from a receipt printer behind the counter, set in the same typeface as the wordmark, so the busiest hour of the morning needs no design decisions at all.

The shop sits in a protected streetscape, so we left the façade alone. A signwriter painted the name in gold leaf on the inside of the glass in a single afternoon, with the opening hours in smaller letters beneath it.
We wanted people to know it was a bakery before they could read the sign. Now there is a queue before we open.
— Lotte Brouwer, founder and head baker

data.title: Lowland Coffee
data.summary: Packaging for a Rotterdam roaster that marks each coffee's altitude on the bag, measured from a roastery below sea level.

$media.alt: A plain brown kraft pouch with a sealed top, lying on a white surface

children.text: Lowland Roasters buy green coffee from eleven farms and roast it in a warehouse in Rotterdam's old port, two metres below sea level. Their coffees change every few weeks, and the old packaging could not keep up: each new origin meant another print run and another box of bags that would never be used.

The identity starts from the roastery's own altitude. Every label carries a single horizontal line, placed to show how far above the roastery each coffee was grown, from 1,200 to 2,100 metres. It is one small piece of information, but it gives every coffee a place on the bag without a map or an illustration.
A label that changes every week

The pouches are blank, unbleached kraft with a compostable liner. Everything that changes sits on one label, printed in runs of two hundred on a small printer at the roastery. We built the templates so the roasters can set up a new coffee in ten minutes without opening design software. Tasting notes are written by the roasters in their own words and kept to three lines.

The same system runs from 250-gram retail pouches to five-kilo wholesale bags and the cups in Lowland's café. The wordmark appears once on each object, always at the foot. Cafés return the wholesale bags, which are washed, relabelled and filled again.
Our coffees change every few weeks. Now the packaging keeps up, and we have not thrown away a single bag.
— Tomas Verhoef, co-founder and head roaster

data.title: Field Quarterly
data.summary: A redesign of an independent quarterly about Dutch farmland: a smaller format, uncoated paper and covers with one photograph.

$media.alt: An open handmade booklet with deckle-edged blank pages on a wooden table in low sunlight

children.text: Field Quarterly has reported on Dutch farming, land and food since 2016. By issue 30 it had grown thick and crowded, and readers told the editors they skimmed it. Field Publishing asked us to redesign the magazine without losing what its regular readers valued: long reporting and patient photography.

We reduced the format to 170 × 240 millimetres, small enough for a coat pocket, and moved to an uncoated, slightly warm stock that takes photographs softly and type sharply. The cover carries one photograph and the issue number. There are no cover lines; the contents page does that job.
A grid with room for notes

Features run in a single wide column with a generous outer margin for captions, sources and the occasional chart. Each one opens on a full-bleed photograph. A serif sets every feature, and a grotesk is kept for numbers, tables and the field reports at the back, which gather each season's yields, prices and rainfall into one table per province.

We now commission two photographers for each issue and brief them on one rule: photograph the land as it is, early in the day, without staging. Every cover since issue 31 has been made before eight in the morning. The contact sheets come back to the studio, and we make the edit with the editors in a single afternoon.
Readers tell us they keep it now. Before the redesign, most of them passed it on.

data.title: Ola Ceramics
data.summary: An online shop for a stoneware studio, organised by kiln firing, with every piece photographed on its own in the same light.

$media.alt: A speckled white stoneware bottle and two small bowls on a white table against a grey wall

children.text: Ola Nowak throws stoneware in a studio in Delfshaven and fires her kiln every five weeks. Each firing yields around 140 pieces, and no two glazes come out quite alike. Her old shop listed products by type with one photograph per design, so customers often received a bowl that looked nothing like the picture.

The new shop is built around the kiln. Each firing becomes a numbered collection that opens on a set date, announced to a waiting list a week before. Past firings stay online as an archive, with sold pieces marked rather than removed, so the shop doubles as a record of the studio's work. Most firings sell out within two days of opening.

We art-directed a photography setup that Ola can run herself in a day: one grey backdrop, one north-facing window, a fixed camera height and a scale reference just out of frame. Each piece is photographed on its own from the same distance, so a cup and a bowl can be compared by size at a glance.

Product pages give height, diameter, weight and capacity, measured for each piece rather than each design. Each listing also carries a short note from Ola on the clay and the glaze. Returns fell by two-thirds in the first year.
People used to email to ask how big a bowl really was. Now they can see it next to everything else.

data.title: Concrete Futures
data.summary: Identity, catalogue and gallery graphics for an exhibition on the reuse of post-war concrete buildings in the Netherlands.

$media.alt: A courtyard of board-marked concrete with stacked volumes, deep openings and a planted ledge

children.text: Concrete Futures, at Het Bouwhuis in Rotterdam, looked at thirty-one post-war concrete buildings in the Netherlands that were adapted rather than demolished: a church that became a library, a car park turned into housing, a grain silo now full of studios. We designed the exhibition identity, the catalogue and the graphics in the galleries.

Every building in the show is drawn at 1:500 and printed at the same size, from a six-storey office block to a bus shelter, so visitors can compare a church with a garage without reading a caption. The drawings also became the campaign: thirty-one posters, one building each, rotated across the city's poster columns during the run.

The 312-page catalogue is bound in black cloth that softens and scuffs with use, much as the buildings do. Photographs and drawings are printed on separate stocks: a smooth paper for the photography and an uncoated one for plans, sections and essays. Each essay is followed by the drawings of the building it discusses, so the book can be read in any order.

Wall texts hang with their centre at 1.35 metres, comfortable for visitors who are standing or seated, and are set large enough to read from two metres away. Every caption repeats the scale bar, so no drawing appears without one. Texts are in Dutch and English at the same size, and neither is set as a translation of the other.
The catalogue sold out before the exhibition closed. That had never happened here before.
— Hanna de Graaf, head of exhibitions, Het Bouwhuis

data.title: Hotel Wilde
data.summary: Identity and wayfinding for a 24-room hotel in a converted 1920s schoolhouse, from the room numbers to the breakfast menu.

$media.alt: A hotel lobby with timber slat walls, a terrazzo floor and groups of low chairs, tables and potted plants

children.text: Hotel Wilde occupies a 1920s schoolhouse in Rotterdam-Kralingen and is named after Johanna Wilde, who ran the school for thirty years. The owners turned twelve classrooms into twenty-four rooms and asked us for an identity that would feel as if it had always belonged to the building.

The school's name is cast into the brickwork above the entrance in tall, narrow capitals. We redrew those letters, completed the alphabet and use it for the wordmark, the room numbers and the signs, with a plain grotesk for anything guests need to read quickly. Letters missing from the façade were drawn from the original building drawings of 1926, which we found in the city archive.

Room numbers are cut from blackened steel and fixed to saddle-leather straps beside each door, at hand height, so they can also be read by touch. Floor numbers are painted straight onto the plaster at the top of each staircase. We tested the numbers with guests who have low vision before the steel was cut. The corridors carry no other signs.
A breakfast menu that changes weekly

Printed matter is kept to a few things: a key fob, a room card, a guest book and a breakfast menu printed every Monday on a risograph in the old staff room. All of them use the same two typefaces and one colour, the green of the school's original doors. The kitchen writes the menu on Sunday evening, and the template does the rest.
Guests photograph the room numbers. We did not expect that, and we like it.
